_comment: Category-level attributes shared across ALL profiles. A profile may not set
tau or decay per category; those derive from these tables. This is what makes
profile construction auditable instead of per-category hand-tuning.
tau derives from trip purpose. decay derives from substitutability.

trip_purpose_distance_m.citation: Rahul, T. M., Manoj, M., Tahlyan, D. & Verma, A. (2021). The Influence of Activities and Socio-Economic/Demographic Factors on the Acceptable Distance in an Indian Scenario. Transportation in Developing Economies 7(1):3. doi:10.1007/s40890-020-00110-3. Table 3.
trip_purpose_distance_m.context: Bangalore household travel survey, 2400 households, 95% confidence / 2% margin of error, Sept 2012 - Mar 2013. Same city as this study.
trip_purpose_distance_m.definition: 'Acceptable distance' is the fitted log-normal threshold beyond which a traveller shifts mode or route. It is NOT a mean trip distance - do not cite the two interchangeably.
caveats: Survey predates most of Bangalore's metro network.
Age was NOT a significant differentiator (all bands pooled at 343 m); trip purpose, gender, income and tenure were. This is why profiles are not built on life stage.

walking_speed_m_per_min.citation: Banerjee, A., Maurya, A. K. & Lammel, G. (2018). A Review of Pedestrian Flow Characteristics and Level of Service over Different Pedestrian Facilities. Collective Dynamics 3:1-52. doi:10.17815/CD.2018.17
walking_speed_m_per_min.value: 80 m/min = 4.8 km/h. The review reports sidewalk free-flow speeds of 65-85 m/min (mean 79) across countries; 80 is the standard planning value and sits at that mean.
walking_speed_m_per_min.why_not_valhalla_default: Valhalla's 5.1 km/h (85 m/min) sits at the CEILING of the observed range. 4.8 km/h gives a 1200 m fifteen-minute reach, matching the ~1200 m assumed across the 15-minute-city literature.
walking_speed_m_per_min.why_not_observed_journey_speed: The survey's mean walking trip (869 m in 24 min) implies 36 m/min, below any measured walking speed. That figure is a ratio of means over skewed distributions and conflates detour, walking speed and delay: 869 m x 1.38 detour = 1199 m network, which at 79 m/min is 15.2 min, leaving 8.8 min (37%) of crossing/waiting/reporting delay. A uniform slowdown would mis-model delay that is concentrated at road crossings.
walking_speed_m_per_min.demographic_multipliers: Same review: males walk 4-9 m/min faster than females; older pedestrians 15-20 m/min slower. An older pedestrian at ~61.5 m/min covers in 15 min what the reference pedestrian covers in ~11.7, so mobility differences map onto tau shifts on the shared grid rather than needing per-profile catchments.
walking_speed_m_per_min.caveat: These are FREE-FLOW speeds - a theoretical maximum excluding crossings and congestion. Catchments therefore represent unimpeded walking and are optimistic against real journeys.

_sources.substitutability: NOT empirically grounded. Derived from functional class as a stated modelling assumption: facilities whose function is fulfilled by one good instance are 'low'; those where variety itself is the benefit are 'high'.

disamenity_buffer_m.citation: Li, Y., Mallinson, P. A. C., Aggarwal, A., Kulkarni, B. & Kinra, S. (2022). Association of Neighborhood Alcohol Environment With Alcohol Intake and Cardiovascular Risk Factors in India: Cross-Sectional Evidence From APCAPS. Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine 9:844086. doi:10.3389/fcvm.2022.844086.
disamenity_buffer_m.context: Indian cohort. Alcohol outlet density within a 400 m buffer of the household was associated with adverse cardiovascular measures, and the association was stronger for the immediate locality than for village-wide availability - so 400 m is an evidenced radius at which proximity to these outlets is consequential in India.
corroboration: Karnataka excise licensing prohibits a liquor outlet within 100 m of an educational or religious institution or hospital, which codifies the same separation but at a distance below both our 250 m cell and our 3-minute minimum threshold, so it motivates rather than parameterises the setting.

Campbell et al. (2009), Am J Prev Med 37(6):556-569, doi:10.1016/j.amepre.2009.09.028: Community Preventive Services Task Force review of 88 studies finding greater outlet density associated with increased consumption and related harms including violence.
